problem.title: Most marketplaces sell promises.
problem.intro: DeeWaanAI was built because the status quo is broken.

items.title: Anyone can upload a prompt
items.body: Most marketplaces have zero quality gates. A listing is a title, a description, and a promise. You have no way to know whether the prompts are well-engineered, quietly broken, or actively malicious.

items.title: Your data goes who-knows-where
items.body: Most platforms run your work on their servers: your inputs, your outputs, and your API keys pass through opaque middlemen. DeeWaanAI runs only on your computer — execution never touches our servers.

items.title: Locked into one chat app
items.body: Force you to abandon the tools you already use and learn a new interface. Handing a colleague a working pipeline means everyone switching to the same app first.

steps.title: Install locally

steps.title: Connect your chat

steps.title: Create, fork, run
steps.body: Build pipelines in chat or with the visual designer, or fork one from the marketplace. Every run goes to your providers under your keys — we never execute anything for you.

items.a: DeeWaanAI is a marketplace for AI pipelines — multi-step AI workflows you can create, share, and fork. Before a listing can be forked, its evidence has to pass structural checks: a completed test recorded by the platform, a judging panel that could not have graded its own work, a scan of the disclosed text for secrets, and the author's consent to the exact preview that went public.

items.q: What is a certified AI pipeline?
items.a: A published pipeline has passed structural checks, not an opinion poll: its test plan completed and recorded by the platform, three judges from three different model developers with none of them a model that generated the answers, every attempt disclosed including the failures, and the seller consenting to the exact public preview. What you get is the record itself — inputs, outputs, the judging prompts in full, every score — so you can judge the evidence rather than a badge.

Install DeeWaanAI on your computer (one setup command), then paste your local MCP URL into any MCP-compatible client — Claude, ChatGPT, Kimi, Cursor, and others. You then create and use pipelines directly from your chat, and everything runs locally on your machine.

items.q: Do I need new API keys?
items.a: You bring your own LLM provider keys. Your pipeline runs go to your providers under your keys — DeeWaanAI orchestrates, it doesn't intercept.

items.q: Is my pipeline IP protected if I share it?
items.a: During evaluation, yes: the judging panel only ever receives the published test inputs and outputs, never your prompts, and nothing is used for training. But sharing itself is open source in the literal sense — anyone who forks your listing receives the pipeline definition itself. Publish only work you are willing to give away.

Nothing. DeeWaanAI is free and open source, and marketplace listings are shared free of charge. Your only cost is your own LLM provider usage: runs go out under your keys, so your provider bills you directly.

items.q: Can I share a pipeline with someone who uses a different AI app?
items.a: Yes. DeeWaanAI is an MCP server, so you each connect your own client — Kimi, Claude, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible app. You lend the pipeline to that one account: by default they can run it and keep the answer without ever reading your prompts, and their run uses their own API keys. Publishing stays with whoever created the work, whatever privilege the share carries.
Research Mode adds batch runs (up to 100 inputs in parallel) and pipeline chaining (feed one pipeline's output into another). It ships in the box — turn it on with a feature flag in Settings.

items.q: What can I do for free?
items.a: Everything. DeeWaanAI is the complete product at no cost: the custom pipeline designer with IF/WHILE loops and quality gates, Human-in-the-Loop approval gates, the AI Auto-Designer, up to 3 of your own LLM providers in one pipeline, and publishing to the marketplace. There is no trimmed tier to grow out of.

IF/WHILE loops let you build conditional and repeating workflow logic — included free, not a paid extra. A quality gate can check an agent's output and automatically loop back until it passes — or route to a different step based on the result.

The AI Auto-Designer lets you describe your goal in plain language — for example, 'turn a product idea into a launch plan' — and the platform automatically generates the optimal pipeline with agents, prompts, quality gates, and approvals. It is included free, like everything else.

steps: Make sure DeeWaanAI is installed and running on your computer (Step 0 above).
Paste the MCP URL above as the connector URL.
Approve the sign-in in your browser when the OAuth window opens (use Chrome if Safari shows a localhost error).

Choose "Add custom connector" and paste the MCP URL.
Complete the OAuth approval in the browser tab that opens.
Start a chat and ask about your pipelines to verify the connection.

clients.name: ChatGPT
steps: Make sure DeeWaanAI is installed and running on your computer (Step 0 above).
Add a new MCP connector and paste the MCP URL.
Approve access in the OAuth window.
Verify by asking ChatGPT to list your DeeWaanAI pipelines.

clients.name: Cursor
steps: Make sure DeeWaanAI is installed and running on your computer (Step 0 above).
Add a new MCP server with the URL above (streamable HTTP).
Complete OAuth in the browser when prompted.
Ask the agent about your pipelines to confirm it works.

clients.name: Generic MCP client
steps: Make sure DeeWaanAI is installed and running on your computer (Step 0 above).
Add the MCP URL as a remote server; the server speaks OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration.
Approve the consent screen once — tokens refresh automatically afterwards.

trust.metaDescription: Every DeeWaanAI listing is published with its full test record — inputs, outputs, the exact judging prompts, every score and every failure — and the checks are structural: a completed platform-recorded plan and a panel that could not have graded its own work. Fail-closed by design.
trust.title: How DeeWaanAI evidence works
trust.intro: Most AI marketplaces sell promises. DeeWaanAI publishes a record you can read. This page explains exactly what has to be true before a pipeline can be shared — and what you can check afterwards.

paragraphs: Every AI marketplace has the same structural flaw: anyone can upload anything. A listing is a title, a description, and a promise. The buyer has no way to know whether the prompts are well-engineered, quietly broken, or actively malicious — until after they have run it.

Some platforms add AI judges. That helps, but an AI grading its peers is gameable: prompt-injection tricks and evaluator-pleasing fluff score well without being good. Others rely on creator self-reviews and star ratings, which measure popularity, not quality.
DeeWaanAI was designed around a different premise: trust must be earned by the pipeline, in layers you can inspect, before anyone is asked to build on it.

The first gate is code, not AI. Every submitted pipeline passes through a deterministic scanner that inspects the actual prompt content for injection phrases, hidden Unicode tricks (zero-width characters, bidirectional overrides, homoglyphs), data-exfiltration patterns, embedded secrets, and PII leaks.

Because the scanner is deterministic, it cannot be charmed, confused, or prompt-injected. A listing that fails is rejected immediately, with the specific findings returned to the creator. No exceptions, no appeals to a language model's mood.

sections.h: Layer 2 — Test runs the creator pays for
paragraphs: Next, the pipeline is run against a suite of generated test inputs — on the creator's own provider account, under their own keys. The platform pays for zero model calls: whoever submits a listing funds its evaluation, so evaluation can never become a hidden cost passed back to users.
Every attempt — including the failures — is recorded to a ledger as it happens. The record that later goes public is assembled from what was actually observed, not reconstructed after the fact.

The final gate is structural, and it is the one that actually matters. Before a listing can be forked, the pipeline is run on a frozen plan of approved test inputs, and its real outputs — not its prompts, not its marketing copy — are scored by a judging panel: three judges from three different model developers, under three different prompt framings, with none of the judges sharing a developer with any model that generated the answers. Self-grading is refused by the gate itself.

Then the record goes public: the exact test inputs, the outputs, the full text of every judging prompt, every score with its rationale, every judgment that failed to parse, what the run cost, and which pieces of cost are still unknown. You are not asked to trust a badge. You are handed the evidence and told what was withheld, if anything — and a listing whose evidence is incomplete, self-graded or leaking a secret simply does not get published.

Every layer errs in the same direction: if anything goes wrong — a scan error, a failed run, an incomplete record — the listing simply stays unpublished. There is no failure mode in which a pipeline accidentally becomes sellable.
This is the opposite of how most platforms treat errors, and it is deliberate. Trust compounds slowly and collapses fast; the system is built to never spend trust it hasn't earned.

sections.h: What this means for creators' IP
paragraphs: During evaluation, secret prompts are never sent to the judges — they receive the published test inputs and outputs only — and they are never used for training. Sharing itself is a choice with no take-backs: a forked listing delivers the pipeline definition itself, open-source. Publish only work you are willing to give away.

The result is a marketplace where creators share work they are proud to stand behind, and anyone who forks a listing gets something no other prompt marketplace offers: the full, signed evidence record behind it — verifiable offline, against the exact version they received.

privacy.metaDescription: What data DeeWaanAI collects, how it is used and stored, and the rights you have over it.
privacy.title: Privacy Policy

paragraphs: This Privacy Policy explains what information {{COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME}} ("we", "us") collects through the DeeWaanAI platform, website, and MCP server (the "Service"), how we use it, and the choices you have.

Account data: your email address, username, and authentication identifiers. Configuration data: pipelines, agents, and settings you create. Credentials: LLM provider API keys you choose to store, which are encrypted at rest and used only to call your providers on your behalf. Usage data: run logs, audit events, and technical telemetry needed to operate and secure the Service.

We use collected data to operate the Service (including executing your pipelines with your providers), to certify marketplace listings, to secure the platform and prevent abuse, and to communicate with you about the Service. We do not sell your personal data, and we do not use your prompts or provider keys to train models.

Pipeline runs send the relevant prompts and inputs to the LLM providers you configured, under your own accounts and keys — this is the core function of the Service. We additionally rely on infrastructure processors (hosting, database, object storage, and payment processing when paid purchases begin) under appropriate data-processing terms.

We retain account and configuration data while your account is active. You may export your data at any time through the platform's data-portability tools, and you may request deletion of your account and associated personal data via {{FALLBACK_EMAIL}}. Backups rotate out on a fixed schedule after deletion.

Depending on your jurisdiction (including the UK and EEA), you may have rights of access, rectification, erasure, portability, restriction, and objection. Contact {{FALLBACK_EMAIL}} to exercise them. You may also lodge a complaint with your local data-protection authority.
We may update this policy from time to time and will post the revised version on this page with a new "last updated" date.
